questions.question: In the Delhi Sultanate, what was the main duty of the "Muqtis" in their assigned iqtas?

options.text: To manage high quality of horses
To lead military campaigns and maintain law and order

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To lead military campaigns and maintain law and order**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Role of Muqtis:** The primary duty of **Muqtis** in the Delhi Sultanate was to lead military campaigns, maintain law and order, and ensure the safety of the assigned territories (iqtas).

• ** The iqta system** was introduced by rulers like **Iltutmish** and developed further by successive sultans. Under this system, territories (iqtas) were allocated to military officers (Muqtis) for governance and revenue collection.

• ** Muqtis were responsible for collecting revenue and taxes from their iqta. A part of the revenue was sent to the central treasury, while the rest was utilized for administrative and military purposes.

• 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• ** 

• The iqta system** was central to the administrative structure of the Delhi Sultanate. It was a system of land revenue and territorial governance that ensured efficient administration and military support.

• The term **iqta** refers to land grants or assignments made to officials in return for administrative and military services.

• The system was initially borrowed from the Islamic world and adapted by Indian rulers like **Iltutmish** during the 13th century.

• Muqtis were appointed to manage these iqtas and were tasked with governance, revenue collection, and military defense.

• ** 

• During the reign of Alauddin Khilji**, the iqta system was reformed to prevent corruption. Muqtis were required to keep detailed accounts of revenues and expenditures.

• In some cases, Muqtis were rotated to different iqtas to ensure loyalty and prevent the establishment of independent power bases.

• ** 

• Muqtis were expected to support the Sultan in major campaigns by providing troops and resources from their iqtas.

• They also acted as intermediaries between the local population and the Sultanate’s central administration.

• 

• Under **Iltutmish**, the iqta system helped consolidate the Sultanate’s control over vast territories by delegating responsibilities to trusted officers.

• During **Ghiyasuddin Balban’s** reign, Muqtis played a crucial role in suppressing rebellions and maintaining stability in remote regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• ** The Sultanate maintained strict control over Muqtis to ensure loyalty and efficiency. Revenue records were regularly audited, and Muqtis who failed in their duties faced severe penalties.

•

questions.question: Who among the following ruled Kashmir during 980 to 1003?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Queen Didda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Queen Didda** ruled Kashmir from **980 to 1003 CE**. She was one of the most prominent female rulers in the history of Kashmir.

• She belonged to the Lohara dynasty and was known for her remarkable administrative skills and political acumen.

• Queen Didda successfully consolidated her power by eliminating rivals and suppressing rebellions during her reign.

• Her reign marked a period of relative stability in Kashmir, and she played a significant role in strengthening the kingdom's foundations.

• She was the widow of King Ksemagupta and ruled as regent for her son and grandson before assuming full control of the throne.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Role in Consolidating Power:** 

• Queen Didda was known for her ability to manage and eliminate internal threats to her power, including the assassination of officials who posed a challenge to her authority.

• She used her political intelligence to maintain control over the kingdom and ensured that her rule was undisputed.

• **Lohara Dynasty:** 

• The Lohara dynasty was a prominent ruling dynasty in Kashmir during medieval times, known for its contributions to art, architecture, and governance.

• Queen Didda played a pivotal role in the early consolidation of the dynasty's rule over Kashmir.

• **Historical Context:** 

• Kashmir during Queen Didda's reign was a culturally rich and strategically important region in northern India.

• Her governance helped protect the kingdom from external invasions and internal instability during her time.

• **Legacy:** 

• Queen Didda is remembered as one of the most powerful and influential female rulers in Indian history.

• Her reign is documented in historical texts as a period of effective administration and centralized governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Other Options:** 

• **Mariam-uz-Zamani:** She was a Mughal queen and mother of Emperor Jahangir. She had no connection with the rule of Kashmir.

• **Khanzada Begum:** A prominent figure in Mughal history, but she did not rule Kashmir.

• **Durgavati:** A Gond queen known for her resistance against Mughal forces, but her rule was limited to central India, not Kashmir.

• **Historical Significance:** Queen Didda’s reign demonstrates the significant role of women in medieval Indian politics and governance.

questions.question: Which article of the Indian constitution is related with power of High Courts to issue certain writs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 226**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 226** of the Indian Constitution empowers the High Courts to issue certain writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for other purposes.
 
• Under this article, High Courts can issue writs such as **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto** to ensure justice and protect individuals' rights.
 
• This provision is broader than **Article 32**, as it includes both fundamental rights and other legal rights, which makes it an important judicial tool.
 
• The jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 is wider and not limited to fundamental rights; it extends to any legal right or issue concerning justice.
 
• High Courts can also exercise this power in cases where the cause of action arises within their territorial jurisdiction, allowing them to address regional legal matters effectively.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 32 of the Constitution:**

 
 
• It empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of **fundamental rights**.
 
• It is considered the "heart and soul" of the Constitution as described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
 
• Unlike Article 226, it is limited to the enforcement of fundamental rights only.
 
 
 
• **Article 227:**
 
 
• This article gives the High Courts the power of **superintendence** over all subordinate courts and tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction.
 
• It ensures judicial discipline and administrative efficiency in lower courts.
 
 
 
• **Article 131:**
 
 
• It deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in disputes between the Government of India and one or more states, or between states.
 
• It is primarily used for resolving federal disputes rather than individual rights.
 
 
 
• **Types of Writs:**
 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** To ensure protection against unlawful detention.
 
• **Mandamus:** To compel a public authority to perform its duty.
 
• **Prohibition:** To prevent lower courts from exceeding their jurisdiction.
 
• **Certiorari:** To transfer a case from a lower court to a higher court or quash an incorrect order.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** To challenge the legality of a person's claim to a public office.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **High Court's Jurisdiction:**

 
 
• High Courts under Article 226 can act in matters involving **fundamental rights** as well as **legal rights**.
 
• This makes their jurisdiction broader compared to the Supreme Court under Article 32.
 
 
 
• **Territorial Scope:**
 
 
• The writ jurisdiction is available within the territorial boundaries of the respective High Court.
 
• It ensures regional justice and legal accountability.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The concept of writs originated in **English Common Law**, later adopted into the Indian legal system.
 
• Writs are a vital tool for upholding the principles of **Rule of Law** in India.

questions.question: Who took oath as Governor of Manipur in January 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hari Babu Kambhampati**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Hari Babu Kambhampati** took oath as the **Governor of Manipur** in **January 2025**. His appointment follows the tradition of appointing individuals with political and administrative experience to the gubernatorial post.

• The oath ceremony was conducted as per the constitutional provisions outlined in **Article 159 of the Constitution of India**, which mandates the Governor to take an oath before assuming office.

• **Hari Babu Kambhampati** is known for his extensive political career and contributions to public administration. He has previously served as a Member of Parliament and has been actively involved in policymaking.

• The Governor plays a crucial role in **maintaining constitutional order** in the state, ensuring the implementation of laws, and serving as a liaison between the state and central governments.

• The appointment of **Hari Babu Kambhampati** aligns with the government’s strategy to place experienced individuals in key positions to facilitate smooth governance and administrative oversight in states like Manipur.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Role of Governors in India:**

• Governors are appointed by the **President of India** under **Article 155** of the Constitution.

• They serve as the **constitutional head** of the state and are responsible for ensuring the state's governance aligns with the Constitution.

• The Governor has the power to summon, prorogue, and dissolve the State Legislative Assembly under **Article 174**.

• Governors act as a bridge between the state and central governments, ensuring effective coordination and communication.

• **Manipur - Key Facts:**

• Manipur is located in the **northeastern region of India** and is known for its rich cultural heritage and biodiversity.

• The state capital is **Imphal**, and it is famous for the **Loktak Lake**, the largest freshwater lake in northeastern India.

• Manipur became a full-fledged state of India on **January 21, 1972**.

• **Constitutional Provisions Related to Governors:**

• **Article 153:** Provides for a Governor in each state.

• **Article 154:** Vests the executive powers of the state in the Governor.

• **Article 161:** Grants the Governor the power to pardon, reprieve, or commute sentences in certain cases.

• **Recent Appointments:**

• Governors are appointed based on their administrative experience, political background, and ability to contribute to governance.

• Appointments in states like Manipur are significant due to the state's strategic location and socio-political challenges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Oath of Office:** The Governor takes an oath to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of India, as prescribed under **Article 159**.

• **Tenure:** The Governor usually serves a term of **5 years**, but this can vary based on political decisions and administrative requirements.

• **Functions:** Governors have legislative, executive, and judicial functions, including assenting to bills, appointing the Chief Minister, and granting pardons.

• **Significance:** The Governor’s role is particularly critical in states with diverse socio-political landscapes, such as Manipur, where maintaining stability and constitutional order is essential.

questions.question: In November 2024, which ministry launched the "Scheme for Strengthening the Medical Device Industry"?

options.text: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers** launched the **"Scheme for Strengthening the Medical Device Industry"** in **November 2024**. 
• This scheme aims to promote **domestic manufacturing** of medical devices and reduce reliance on imports, thereby achieving self-reliance under the vision of **Aatmanirbhar Bharat**. 
• The initiative focuses on creating **common infrastructure facilities** and providing **financial assistance** to strengthen the medical device industry in India. 
• The scheme is part of the government’s efforts to enhance the **competitiveness, quality, and affordability** of medical devices produced in India. 
• It aligns with the government's commitment to boost the **Make in India** initiative, specifically targeting the healthcare and medical device sectors. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Medical Device Industry in India:** 
• The Indian medical device sector is one of the **fastest-growing industries**, with an annual growth rate of approximately **15%**. 
• India ranks among the **top 20 global markets** for medical devices. 
• The sector encompasses a wide range of products, including diagnostic equipment, imaging systems, implants, and surgical instruments. 
• The government has been focusing on **regulatory reforms** to ensure the quality and safety of domestically produced medical devices. 
• **Make in India Initiative:** 
• Launched in **2014** by the Government of India, this initiative aims to transform India into a global manufacturing hub. 
• The medical device industry is a **key focus area** under this initiative to reduce import dependency and boost local production. 
• Emphasis is placed on promoting **research and development (R&D)** in the medical device sector. 
• **Role of the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers:** 
• The ministry oversees the **Pharmaceuticals Department**, which is responsible for the medical device sector. 
• It plays a crucial role in formulating policies to **support domestic industries** and regulate imports and exports. 
• Through schemes like this, the ministry aims to create a globally competitive ecosystem for medical device manufacturing in India. 
• **Global Context:** 
• The global medical device market is expected to reach **USD 800 billion** by 2030, making this initiative timely and crucial for India’s participation in the global market. 
• Countries like the **USA, Germany, and Japan** lead in medical device manufacturing, but India is emerging as a strong competitor due to its cost advantages. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Significance of the Scheme:** 
• The scheme aims to reduce India’s **70-80% dependency** on imported medical devices. 
• It will promote the establishment of **medical device parks** with state-of-the-art infrastructure to support domestic manufacturers. 
• By fostering innovation, the initiative is expected to enhance **export potential** and improve the global competitiveness of Indian medical devices. 
• **Challenges Addressed:** 
• The scheme tackles issues like **high import costs**, lack of infrastructure, and limited access to advanced technologies in the medical device sector. 
• It also encourages **collaboration between industry and academia** to promote R&D and skill development.

questions.question: Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) is conducted by which institution in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**NSO (National Statistical Office)**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)** is conducted by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**, which functions under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)** in India. 
• The **PLFS** was launched in **April 2017** to provide reliable and timely estimates of key labour market indicators, such as employment and unemployment. 
• It replaced the earlier system of quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Surveys (EUS), aiming to provide annual estimates for both rural and urban areas and quarterly estimates for urban areas. 
• The survey collects data on the **Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR), Worker Population Ratio (WPR), and Unemployment Rate (UR)** in the country. 
• The data gathered is crucial for policymaking, employment generation strategies, and understanding the socio-economic conditions of workers in India. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **National Statistical Office (NSO):** 
• The NSO was formed in **2019** by merging the **Central Statistics Office (CSO)** and the **National Sample Survey Office (NSSO).** 
• It is the **apex body** for statistical activities and the official data collection agency of the Government of India. 
• Its responsibilities include conducting nationwide surveys, such as the **PLFS**, Consumer Expenditure Surveys, and Agriculture Surveys. 
• **Objectives of PLFS:** 
• To measure the **Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR)**, which is the percentage of the population actively participating in the labour force. 
• To determine the **Worker Population Ratio (WPR)**, which indicates the proportion of employed persons in the population. 
• To assess the **Unemployment Rate (UR)**, which refers to the percentage of people in the labour force who are unemployed and actively seeking work. 
• **Other Options Explained:** 
• **Development Intelligence Unit:** This is not a recognized body for conducting labour force surveys in India. 
• **Ministry of Labour and Employment:** While this ministry works on labour laws and employment schemes, it does not conduct the PLFS. 
• **NITI Aayog:** NITI Aayog, being a policy think tank, advises on strategies for national development but does not directly conduct surveys like the PLFS. 
• **Importance of PLFS Data:** 
• The data helps in understanding **sectoral employment trends**, such as agriculture, industry, and services. 
• It aids in framing evidence-based policies for addressing **unemployment** and improving **labour market efficiency.** 
• It provides insights into the **gender gap** in workforce participation and other socio-economic disparities. ``

questions.question: Who wrote the book "A Suitable Boy" which was published in 1993?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vikram Seth**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The book "**A Suitable Boy**" was authored by **Vikram Seth**, an Indian novelist and poet, and it was first published in **1993**. 
• This novel is one of the **longest single-volume books** ever published in the English language, with nearly **1,500 pages** in its paperback edition. 
• The story is set in post-Independence, post-Partition **India** and revolves around the efforts of a mother to find a "suitable boy" for her daughter, Lata. 
• The novel explores a wide range of themes, including **family, love, politics, religion**, and the social changes happening in India during the **1950s**. 
• "A Suitable Boy" has been acclaimed for its **rich character development**, detailed portrayal of Indian society, and its ability to weave in complex socio-political issues. 
• It was later adapted into a television drama series by the BBC, directed by **Mira Nair**, and released in **2020**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Vikram Seth:** 
• **Born:** 20 June 1952 in **Calcutta, India**. 
• He is an **Indian author** widely known for his novels, poetry, and works in other literary genres. 
• His other notable works include "**The Golden Gate**" (a novel in verse) and "**An Equal Music**". 
• He has won several awards, including the **Padma Shri** in 2001 and the **WH Smith Literary Award**. 
• **Plot Summary of A Suitable Boy:** 
• The novel's central plot revolves around **Lata Mehra**, a university student, and her mother Rupa's efforts to find her a suitable husband. 
• It also delves into the lives of four families: the Mehras, the Kapoors, the Khans, and the Chatterjis. 
• It captures the **cultural and political atmosphere** of India in the early years after Independence, including themes like the rise of socialism and the Hindu-Muslim divide. 
• The book emphasizes the **importance of individual choice** and personal happiness against societal expectations. 
• **Other Options Explained:** 
• **Amit Varma:** An Indian writer and journalist, known for his blog "**India Uncut**" and the novel "**My Friend Sancho**," but he is not the author of "A Suitable Boy." 
• **Aruni Kashyap:** An Indian writer and translator known for works like "**The House With a Thousand Stories**," but not associated with "A Suitable Boy." 
• **Ajay K Pandey:** An Indian author known for writing romance novels like "**You Are the Best Wife**," but he did not write "A Suitable Boy." 
• **Critical Reception:** 
• "A Suitable Boy" was widely praised for its **epic scope**, intricate storytelling, and its ability to provide a **panoramic view of Indian society**. 
• It has been translated into several languages and remains one of the most celebrated works in Indian-English literature. 
• The novel has often been compared to the works of **Charles Dickens** and **Leo Tolstoy** for its broad scope and detailed character portrayals. </ul

questions.question: Who was the architect behind the design of the India Gate?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Edwin Lutyens**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Edwin Lutyens** was the architect responsible for designing the **India Gate**, which is a war memorial located in New Delhi, India.

• The **India Gate** was built to commemorate the soldiers of the **British Indian Army** who lost their lives during **World War I** and the **Third Anglo-Afghan War**.

• Construction of the India Gate began in **1921** and was completed in **1931**. The foundation stone was laid by the then **Duke of Connaught**.

• The structure is 42 meters high and is made of **Bharatpur red sandstone**. It is an iconic symbol of **colonial architecture** in India.

• The design of the India Gate reflects a combination of **classical European architecture** and elements of Indian art and culture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Edwin Lutyens:**

• Lutyens was a renowned British architect, celebrated for his role in designing **New Delhi**, which became the capital of India in **1931**.

• He worked extensively on the design of **Rashtrapati Bhavan** (formerly the Viceroy's House) and several other key buildings in the city.

• Lutyens' architectural style combined **classical European influences** with elements of Indian design, creating a unique blend that remains iconic today.

• **India Gate:**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: "Navroz festival" is celebrated by which religious community in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Parsi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Navroz**, also known as **Nowruz**, is the **New Year festival** celebrated by the **Parsis** in India and Zoroastrians worldwide.

• The festival marks the beginning of the **Persian New Year** and is celebrated on the **spring equinox**, usually falling on **March 20 or 21**.

• It has its roots in **Zoroastrianism**, one of the world's oldest religions, which originated in ancient Persia (modern-day Iran).

• Navroz is considered a time of **renewal, joy, and purification**. It celebrates the arrival of spring and the renewal of nature.

• In India, the Parsi community observes Navroz with **prayers, feasts, and charitable activities**. They visit the **Fire Temple** (Agiary) to offer prayers and seek blessings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Zoroastrianism:** 

• Zoroastrianism is an ancient religion founded by **Prophet Zoroaster** in Persia around the **6th-7th century BCE**.

• The religion emphasizes the concepts of **good thoughts, good words, and good deeds**.

• Fire is a central element in Zoroastrian worship, symbolizing **purity and the presence of God**.

• **Parsis in India:**

• The Parsis are a small yet significant community in India who migrated from Persia to escape religious persecution around the **8th-10th century CE**.

• They settled primarily in **Gujarat** and **Mumbai** and have contributed immensely to India’s industrial, cultural, and social development.

• **Celebrations of Navroz:**

• Navroz begins with the cleaning and decoration of homes, symbolizing the removal of negativity and a fresh start.

• A traditional feast includes dishes like **sev (sweet vermicelli), pulao, and fish**. Special sweets such as **ravo** and **falooda** are also prepared.

• People wear new clothes and exchange **gifts and greetings** to foster community bonding.

• **Global Observance:**

• Navroz is not limited to Parsis but is also celebrated by **other communities** such as **Kurdish, Persian, and Central Asian cultures**.

• The **United Nations** recognizes March 21 as the **International Day of Nowruz**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Religious Significance:** Navroz holds deep spiritual significance for Zoroastrians as it symbolizes the triumph of **light over darkness** and **good over evil**.

• **Preparation:** The festival involves rituals like **spring cleaning**, wearing new clothes, and preparing a table called **Haft-Seen** with symbolic items like fruits, candles, and mirrors.

• **Parsis in India:** Despite being a small community, the Parsis have significantly influenced India in fields like **business, arts, and philanthropy**. Prominent figures include **Jamshedji Tata** and **Dadabhai Naoroji**.

questions.question: In the context of launch vehicles of India, which of the following launch vehicle is also known as GSLV MK-III?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**LVM3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **LVM3**, also known as **GSLV MK-III**, is India's heaviest and most advanced launch vehicle developed by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**.
 
• LVM3 stands for **Launch Vehicle Mark-3** and is capable of carrying payloads of up to **4 tons to Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO)** and **10 tons to Low Earth Orbit (LEO)**.
 
• This launch vehicle employs a **cryogenic upper stage** (C25 engine) that uses liquid hydrogen as fuel and liquid oxygen as an oxidizer, making it highly efficient.
 
• LVM3 is primarily used for launching heavy communication satellites and has been instrumental in missions like **Chandrayaan-2** and **Gaganyaan (Human Spaceflight Program)**.
 
• The vehicle has three stages: a **solid rocket booster (S200)**, a **liquid core stage (L110)**, and a cryogenic upper stage (C25).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **ASLV (Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle):**

 
 
• ASLV was developed by ISRO in the **1980s** to bridge the gap between the Satellite Launch Vehicle (SLV) and the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV).
 
• It was primarily used to demonstrate satellite launch capability in **Low Earth Orbit (LEO)**.
 
• Its payload capacity was limited to **150 kg**, making it suitable for small experimental satellites.
 
• Though the ASLV program was discontinued, it laid the foundation for more advanced launch vehicles like PSLV and GSLV.
 
 
 
• **SLV-3 (Satellite Launch Vehicle-3):**
 
 
• SLV-3 was India's first experimental satellite launch vehicle, developed in the **1970s and 1980s**.
 
• It successfully launched the satellite **Rohini RS-1** in **1980**, marking India's entry into space exploration.
 
• It had a payload capacity of **40 kg** to LEO and was powered by solid propulsion technology.
 
• SLV-3 paved the way for subsequent advancements in India's space program.
 
 
 
• **PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle):**
 
 
• PSLV is known as the "workhorse" of ISRO, used primarily for launching satellites into **Polar Sun-Synchronous Orbits**.
 
• First launched in **1993**, PSLV has an impressive track record, successfully launching more than **300 satellites** from various countries.
 
• It is a versatile vehicle capable of deploying satellites into various orbits, including **Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO)**.
 
• PSLV played a critical role in missions like **Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)** and **Chandrayaan-1**.
 
 
 
• **GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle):**
 
 
• GSLV is used for launching heavier satellites into **Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO)**.
 
• It incorporates a **cryogenic upper stage**, making it suitable for deploying communication satellites.
 
• GSLV has been used in missions like **GSAT series satellites** and played a key role in **Chandrayaan-2**.
 
• It was developed after PSLV to meet India's growing demand for launching heavier payloads.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **GSLV MK-III Achievements:**

 
 
• Successfully launched **GSAT-19** in **2017**, marking its operational debut.
 
• Used in the launch of **Chandrayaan-2** in **2019**, showcasing its capability for interplanetary missions.
 
• Plays a pivotal role in India's **Gaganyaan Program**, which aims to send humans to space.
 
• Its payload capacity makes it comparable to international heavy-lift rockets.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of LVM3:**
 
 
• Incorporates advanced propulsion systems for higher efficiency.
 
• Offers modular design for flexibility in payload configurations.
 
• Demonstrates India's capability to compete globally in space technology.
 
• Supports strategic applications, including national defense and communication.

• **Pressure** is defined as the force acting per unit area and is mathematically expressed as **Pressure = Thrust / Area**. It is measured in units like Pascals (**Pa**). 
• The formula indicates that **pressure** increases if the **thrust** increases, provided the area remains constant. 
• Conversely, if the **area increases** while the thrust remains constant, the pressure decreases due to the inverse relationship.

questions.question: In the context of reform policy introduced in and after 1991, the investment limit in foreign banks was raised to around ______ as part of financial sector reform.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.74**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• As part of the **financial sector reforms** introduced in and after **1991**, the Indian government liberalized several policies to attract **foreign investment** and improve the efficiency of the financial system.
 
• One significant reform was raising the **foreign investment limit** in the banking sector, specifically for foreign banks operating in India.
 
• The investment cap for foreign banks was increased to **74%**, allowing **greater foreign participation** in the Indian banking sector.
 
• This policy change aimed to modernize the banking sector, increase **competition**, and bring in global expertise in banking operations.
 
• The decision to allow up to **74% foreign direct investment (FDI)** was regulated under the **automatic route**, requiring minimal bureaucratic intervention.
 
• The reform was part of the **New Economic Policy of 1991**, which focused on liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Banking:**

 
 
• FDI in the banking sector is allowed under two segments: private sector banks and public sector banks.
 
• For **private sector banks**, FDI up to **74%** is permitted under the **automatic route**, subject to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) approval in certain cases.
 
• For **public sector banks**, FDI is restricted to **20%**, and this requires government approval.
 
• The policy aims to infuse foreign capital, increase global expertise, and enhance operational efficiency.
 
 
 
• **New Economic Policy of 1991:**
 
 
• Introduced by the then Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh** under the leadership of Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao**.
 
• The reforms emphasized **liberalization**, **privatization**, and **globalization** (LPG model).
 
• The policy aimed to address the **balance of payments crisis** and improve the economic growth rate by reducing state control over industries and encouraging private sector participation.
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Regulations:**
 
 
• The RBI plays a key role in regulating FDI in the banking sector to ensure financial stability.
 
• It monitors compliance with the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and other relevant legislations.
 
• RBI approval is required for certain banking activities involving foreign investment, particularly for mergers, acquisitions, and setting up new branches.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Increasing FDI Limit:**
 
 
• Allowed foreign banks to establish a stronger presence in India, fostering **global competition** in the domestic market.
 
• Improved access to **advanced banking technology** and **international best practices**.
 
• Enhanced the availability of financial services, especially in urban areas, while creating a more competitive and efficient banking environment.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Automatic Route:** This refers to a process where foreign investors do not require prior approval from the government or RBI for making investments in certain sectors.
 
• **Banking Regulation Act, 1949:** The law that governs all banking operations in India, ensuring sound financial practices and protecting depositors' interests.
 
• **Liberalization:** The process of reducing government-imposed restrictions and regulations to encourage private sector investment and economic growth.
 
• **Globalization:** The integration of domestic economies with the global economy, leading to an increase in cross-border trade, investment, and cultural exchange.

questions.question: Ujjain expanded under the patronage of which Maratha chief?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sindhia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ujjain**, an ancient city located in Madhya Pradesh, expanded significantly under the **patronage of the Maratha chief Daulat Rao Sindhia**. He was a prominent leader of the Sindhia dynasty and played a crucial role in the city's development.
 
• The Sindhia dynasty held significant influence over the **Malwa region**, which includes Ujjain, during the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Ujjain became a major cultural and administrative center during their reign.
 
• Daulat Rao Sindhia's patronage contributed to the enhancement of Ujjain's infrastructure, including the development of roads, temples, and administrative buildings. His efforts helped in modernizing the city.
 
• Under Sindhia's rule, Ujjain regained its prominence as a center of **Hindu pilgrimage**, with the reconstruction of several temples and the promotion of religious activities.
 
• The Sindhias were known for their association with art, culture, and architecture, which was reflected in the city's growth during their reign. **Ujjain flourished economically and culturally** under their leadership.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Holkar Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Holkars were another prominent Maratha dynasty based in Indore, Madhya Pradesh. Although they contributed to the development of various regions, their influence was primarily centered around Indore, rather than Ujjain.
 
• The Holkar rulers, such as Ahilyabai Holkar, were known for their contributions to temple construction and social welfare, but Ujjain's major development is attributed to Sindhia.
 
 
 
• **Gaekwad Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Gaekwads ruled over Baroda (modern-day Vadodara) in Gujarat and were known for their contributions to the region's prosperity. Their influence did not extend to Ujjain.
 
• They were recognized for their efforts in promoting education and public welfare in their territory.
 
 
 
• **Bhonsle Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Bhonsle dynasty was centered around Nagpur and had significant influence in Maharashtra. Their contributions were largely confined to their domain and did not directly impact Ujjain's development.
 
• They were known for their military prowess and administrative capabilities.
 
 
 
• **Sindhia Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Sindhia dynasty emerged as a powerful Maratha clan with control over large parts of northern and central India, including the Malwa region, where Ujjain is located.
 
• They were instrumental in the political and cultural development of Ujjain, making it a key center during their reign.
 
• Daulat Rao Sindhia's tenure was marked by significant infrastructural improvements and cultural revival in the city.
 
• The Sindhias were also notable for their diplomatic relations with the British during the colonial era.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ujjain's historical significance:**

 
 
• Ujjain has been one of the most important cities in Indian history, particularly as a center of trade, religion, and learning.
 
• It is famous for being the location of the **Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga**, one of the twelve sacred Jyotirlingas in Hindu tradition.
 
• The city has been a major hub for **astronomy and mathematics**, with historical figures such as Varahamihira and Brahmagupta associated with it.
 
 
 
• **Role of Maratha Chiefs:**
 
 
• The Maratha chiefs, including Sindhia, Holkar, Gaekwad, and Bhonsle, played key roles in shaping the history and development of central and western India.
 
• Each of these dynasties contributed uniquely to their respective regions, focusing on infrastructure, art, culture, and governance.
 
• The Sindhia dynasty's influence over Ujjain stands out due to their strategic and cultural investments in the city.

questions.question: The revolt of 1857 was started by the sepoys from which of the following places?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Meerut**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Revolt of 1857**, also known as India’s First War of Independence, began on **May 10, 1857**, in the town of **Meerut**, located in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

• The revolt was triggered by the grievances of the **sepoys (Indian soldiers)** employed under the British East India Company, particularly due to the introduction of the controversial **Enfield rifle**.

• The new rifle cartridges were rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat, which offended both **Hindus (who consider the cow sacred)** and **Muslims (who regard the pig as unclean)**.

• In Meerut, 85 sepoys of the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry refused to use the cartridges and were subsequently court-martialed and imprisoned. This act of punishment outraged their comrades and sparked a rebellion.

• On the night of May 10, 1857, the sepoys in Meerut rose in rebellion, broke into the jail to free their comrades, and marched towards **Delhi**, where they declared the Mughal Emperor **Bahadur Shah II** as their leader.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Causes of the Revolt:**

• **Political Causes:** The annexation policies of the British (e.g., the Doctrine of Lapse) alienated many Indian rulers.

• **Economic Causes:** Heavy taxation, the destruction of traditional industries, and the exploitation of resources led to widespread poverty.

• **Social and Religious Causes:** The British imposed reforms and practices that were perceived as an attack on Indian social and religious traditions.

• **Military Causes:** Discrimination in pay, promotion, and treatment of Indian sepoys compared to their British counterparts created resentment.

• **Course of the Revolt:**

• After starting in Meerut, the revolt spread to various parts of northern and central India, including **Delhi, Kanpur, Jhansi, and Lucknow**.

• Key leaders included **Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi**, **Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh**, and **Tantia Tope**.

• Despite initial successes, the lack of coordination, resources, and modern weaponry led to the revolt's failure by 1858.

• **Consequences of the Revolt:**

• The British Crown assumed direct control over India, ending the rule of the East India Company.

• The policy of annexation was abandoned, and greater respect was given to Indian customs and traditions.

• Reforms were introduced in the Indian Army to prevent future revolts, including increasing the proportion of British soldiers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Significance of Meerut:** The revolt in Meerut marked the beginning of a widespread anti-colonial movement and was a turning point in Indian history.

• **Delhi’s Role:** The sepoys’ decision to march to Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah II as the Emperor of India symbolized a unifying attempt to restore Indian rule.

• **British Response:** The British took about a year to suppress the rebellion, deploying reinforcements and employing brutal measures to crush resistance.

• **Legacy:** Although the revolt failed, it sowed the seeds for future movements for independence, inspiring subsequent generations of freedom fighters.

a7:T

questions.question: Which of the following article of Indian constitution deals with the definition of money bill?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 110**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 110** of the **Indian Constitution** defines a **Money Bill**. It specifies the provisions under which a Bill can be classified as a Money Bill.
 
• A Money Bill includes provisions related to **taxation, borrowing of money by the government, expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, or custody of funds in the Public Account of India**.
 
• A Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill only if it deals exclusively with matters listed in Article 110, including **the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of taxes**.
 
• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has the exclusive authority to decide whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, and their decision is considered final.
 
• Money Bills can only be introduced in the **Lok Sabha**, not in the Rajya Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Money Bill. It can only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may or may not accept.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Difference Between Money Bill and Financial Bill:**

 
 
• A **Money Bill** is defined under **Article 110** and deals exclusively with matters specified therein. A **Financial Bill**, on the other hand, has provisions related to revenue but does not exclusively deal with matters listed under Article 110.
 
• While a Money Bill can only be introduced in the **Lok Sabha**, Financial Bills can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
 
• The Speaker certifies a Bill as a Money Bill, while Financial Bills do not require such certification.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions for Money Bill:**
 
 
• **Article 109**: Discusses the procedure for passing a Money Bill in Parliament.
 
• **Article 117**: Deals with Financial Bills other than Money Bills.
 
• **Article 112**: Refers to the Annual Financial Statement (Budget), which may include Money Bills.
 
 
 
• **Process of Passing Money Bill:**
 
 
• Introduced only in the **Lok Sabha**.
 
• Once passed by the Lok Sabha, it is sent to the **Rajya Sabha**, which can only make recommendations within 14 days.
 
• The Lok Sabha can accept or reject the recommendations, and the Bill is considered passed even if the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days.
 
• After being passed by both Houses (or only the Lok Sabha effectively), the Bill is sent for the **President's assent**.
 
 
 
• **Important Examples of Money Bills:**
 
 
• The **Goods and Services Tax (GST) Bill** was passed as a Money Bill in 2017.
 
• Other examples include Bills related to income tax amendments, appropriation of funds, and public borrowing.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 110** is crucial for maintaining the separation of powers between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha regarding financial legislation.
 
• The Speaker's decision on classifying a Bill as a Money Bill is final and cannot be challenged in court.
 
• This provision ensures that financial matters remain under the control of the directly elected representatives of the people in the Lok Sabha.
 
• Money Bills are an integral part of India's parliamentary democracy, where the government requires legislative approval to impose taxes or spend public funds.
 
• Understanding the provisions of Article 110 is essential for comprehending the legislative process concerning financial matters in India.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of Non-Ferrous metallic mineral?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bauxite**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Bauxite** is a prime example of a **non-ferrous metallic mineral**. It is an ore of aluminum, which is a non-ferrous metal. 
• Non-ferrous metals like aluminum are characterized by the absence of iron, making them resistant to corrosion and lightweight. 
• Bauxite is primarily composed of minerals such as **gibbsite, boehmite, and diaspore**, which are rich in aluminum content. 
• This mineral is extensively used in industries for manufacturing **aircraft, automobiles, electrical appliances, packaging materials**, and construction. 
• Bauxite deposits are found in various countries, with India being a major producer. Significant bauxite reserves in India are located in **Odisha, Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Jharkhand**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Non-Ferrous Metals:** 
• Non-ferrous metals are metals that do not contain iron. Examples include **aluminum, copper, lead, zinc, nickel, titanium, and precious metals like gold and silver**. 
• These metals are known for their **lightweight, corrosion resistance, and high conductivity**, making them essential in various industries. 
• **Characteristics of Bauxite:** 
• **Age:** Bauxite deposits are often formed through laterization during tropical and subtropical conditions over millions of years. 
• **Location:** Globally, bauxite reserves are found in countries like Australia, Guinea, Brazil, and India. 
• **Uses:** Primarily used for aluminum production; also used in refractory materials, abrasives, and cement industries. 
• **Other Mineral Examples:** 
• **Manganese:** A ferrous metallic mineral used in steel production and as an alloying element. 
• **Iron Ore:** A ferrous metallic mineral used in the manufacturing of steel and iron products. 
• **Chromite:** A ferrous metallic mineral used in the production of stainless steel and as a refractory material. 
• **India's Bauxite Production:** 
• India ranks among the top producers of bauxite globally, contributing significantly to the aluminum industry. 
• Major bauxite mines include **Panchpatmali in Odisha**, **Kolhapur in Maharashtra**, and **Kutch in Gujarat**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Bauxite Mining Process:** 
• Bauxite is mined through open-pit mining techniques. 
• The process involves stripping the topsoil and extracting bauxite ore from deposits. 
• Post-extraction, bauxite undergoes refining to produce alumina, followed by smelting to obtain aluminum. 
• **Global Reserves:** 
• Australia is the largest producer of bauxite, with significant reserves in Guinea, Brazil, and India. 
• Guinea holds the world's largest bauxite reserves, accounting for over **40 billion metric tons**. 
• **Environmental Impact:** 
• Bauxite mining can lead to deforestation, loss of biodiversity, and soil erosion. 
• Reclamation efforts and sustainable practices are crucial to mitigate environmental damage. </ul

questions.question: In the context of Indian economy, which of the following is included in the factor cost?

options.text: Only the payment to factors of production
Both the product and production taxes

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only the payment to factors of production**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Factor Cost** refers to the total cost of production, which includes payments made to the **factors of production** such as land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
 
• It is calculated as the sum of all **factor payments** like wages, rent, interest, and profits, excluding any taxes or subsidies imposed by the government.
 
• **Production taxes** and **product taxes** are not included in the calculation of factor cost. Instead, they are included in market price calculations. Hence, options referring to taxes are incorrect.
 
• **Factor cost** is a measure of the cost incurred by producers in producing goods and services and does not consider tax-related influences, making it a more accurate measure of production cost.

questions.question:
Vessels are part of which of the following plant tissue?

I. Xylem

II. Phloem
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vessels are a key component of the xylem tissue** in vascular plants. They are specialized cells responsible for transporting water and nutrients from the roots to other parts of the plant.
 
• **Phloem tissue does not contain vessels;** instead, it contains sieve tubes and companion cells, which are responsible for transporting food (mainly sugars) produced during photosynthesis.
 
• **Xylem vessels are elongated tubular structures** that form a continuous network, facilitating efficient water conduction. They are dead at maturity and lack cytoplasm, allowing unimpeded water flow.
 
• **Vessels are unique to angiosperms,** although some gymnosperms and pteridophytes have tracheids instead of vessels for water conduction.
 
• ***Hence, vessels are part of xylem tissue only.*** Statement I is correct, while Statement II is incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Xylem Tissue:**

 
 
• It is a vascular tissue responsible for the transport of water and dissolved minerals in plants.
 
• Xylem consists of four types of cells: **vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma,** and **xylem fibers.**
 
• Vessels are more efficient in water conduction compared to tracheids due to their larger diameter and interconnected structure.
 
 
 
• **Phloem Tissue:**
 
 
• Phloem is a vascular tissue involved in the transport of organic nutrients, primarily sucrose, from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
 
• Its components include **sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma,** and **phloem fibers.**
 
• Unlike xylem, phloem cells are living, with sieve tube elements lacking a nucleus but relying on companion cells for their functions.
 
 
 
• **Comparison between Xylem and Phloem:**
 
 
• **Direction of transport:** Xylem transports water and minerals upward (roots to shoots), while phloem transports food in multiple directions.
 
• **Cell types:** Xylem contains vessels and tracheids (dead at maturity), whereas phloem contains sieve tubes and companion cells (living).
 
• **Functional role:** Xylem provides mechanical support to the plant, while phloem is involved in nutrient distribution.
 
 
 
• **Vessels vs. Tracheids:**
 
 
• Vessels are wide, cylindrical cells with open ends, forming continuous tubes, while tracheids are narrow, elongated cells with tapered ends.
 
• Vessels are more efficient in water conduction, whereas tracheids provide better mechanical support.
 
• Tracheids are found in both angiosperms and gymnosperms, but vessels are predominantly found in angiosperms.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Development of vessels:** During their development, vessel elements lose their cytoplasm and organelles, becoming hollow and dead, which optimizes water transport.
 
• **Structure of vessels:** Vessel walls are thickened with lignin, a substance that provides structural support and prevents collapse under water pressure.
 
• **Role in plant growth:** Efficient water conduction by vessels is crucial for maintaining turgor pressure, which supports plant growth and stability.
 
• **Study of vascular tissues:** The study of xylem and phloem is a fundamental aspect of botany and contributes to understanding plant physiology and adaptations.

questions.question: What is the result of the uneven growth of the tendril in response to touch?

options.text: The tendril circles around the object and clings to it
The tendril falls off the plant

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The tendril circles around the object and clings to it**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Tendrils** are specialized plant structures that help plants climb and support themselves by attaching to nearby objects, such as a trellis or neighboring plants. 
• When a tendril comes in contact with an object, cells on the side touching the object grow slower, while cells on the opposite side elongate faster. This uneven growth causes the tendril to **curl around the object**. 
• This process is a type of growth movement in response to touch, known as **thigmotropism**. It enables plants to maximize sunlight exposure by climbing toward light sources. 
• The coiling around the object strengthens the plant's anchorage and prevents the tendril from falling off, ensuring stability. 
• Examples of plants with tendrils include **pea plants (Pisum sativum)**, **grapevines (Vitis vinifera)**, and **cucumber plants (Cucumis sativus)**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Thigmotropism:** 
• It is a plant's directional growth response to touch or physical contact with a solid object. 
• In tendrils, this response is facilitated by differential growth rates in cells on opposite sides of the tendril. 
• Other examples of thigmotropism include the coiling of climbing plants such as ivy and the folding of leaves in **Mimosa pudica** when touched. 
• **Types of Tropisms:** 
• **Phototropism:** Growth movement in response to light (e.g., sunflower turning toward sunlight). 
• **Geotropism:** Growth movement in response to gravity (e.g., roots growing downward). 
• **Hydrotropism:** Growth movement in response to water (e.g., roots growing toward water sources). 
• **Thigmotropism:** Growth in response to touch (e.g., tendrils coiling around objects). 
• **Functions of Tendrils:** 
• Provide structural support to weak-stemmed plants. 
• Help plants climb and reach sunlight for photosynthesis. 
• Reduce the risk of being overshadowed by competing vegetation. 
• **Examples of Tendril-Bearing Plants:** 
• **Pea plant (Pisum sativum):** Has leaf tendrils to support climbing. 
• **Grapevine (Vitis vinifera):** Uses tendrils for attachment and climbing. 
• **Passionflower (Passiflora):** Features tendrils for structural support. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Key Characteristics of Tendrils:** 
• Tendrils may originate from leaves, leaflets, or stems depending on the plant species. 
• They are highly sensitive to touch, allowing them to detect and respond to nearby objects. 
• Once coiled, tendrils develop lignin to strengthen their structure and hold the plant securely. 
• **Scientific Explanation:** 
• The coiling is driven by differential auxin distribution. **Auxin**, a plant hormone, accumulates on the side away from the contact point, promoting cell elongation and causing curvature. 
• Other hormones like **ethylene** may also play a role in regulating thigmotropic responses. </ul
